source.title: Emergence of psychopathological computations in large language models
source.authors: Soo-Yong Lee; Hyunjin Hwang; Taekwang Kim; Yuyeong Kim; K. Park; Jaemin Yoo; D. Borsboom; Kijung Shin

record.tranche_reason: The paper is read in full but does not test or rely on the claimed held-out-loss power laws or compute-optimal allocation. It cites Kaplan et al. in connection with model capability, while its own size-related results concern psychopathology computations.
record.gate_note: The study reports how psychopathology-related activation, structural, and behavioral measures vary with LLM size. It does not measure held-out cross-entropy loss, fit loss power laws, test extrapolation from smaller runs, or examine compute-optimal parameter/token allocation. Its own size-scaling results are recorded under fits_no_version; the cited scaling-law results are not extracted as study findings.
record.test_reason: The study measures psychopathology-related feature activations, SCM density and resistance to corrective instructions across 12 open-weight LLMs of different sizes. It reports no held-out loss, no loss power-law fits, no extrapolation, no compute-optimal allocation, no architecture-shape effects on loss, and no standard downstream benchmark scaling. Kaplan et al. is cited only to explain why larger models follow instructions better (Sec. 4.6).
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that network-theoretic psychopathological computations may have emerged in LLMs, and that their structure becomes denser and their functions (resistance) stronger with size. They add that models below 4B mostly show the opposite resistance pattern, which they read as a shift from maintaining semantic coherence. They draw no conclusions about loss scaling.
record.recipe_differences: The study investigates psychopathology-related computations rather than measuring the loss-scaling methods in the original sources.

fits_no_version.finding: Step-50 mean activations, lag-1 correlation magnitude and SCM density increased with LLM size across 12 models (Fig. 2G, polynomial fits).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Psychopathology-related internal feature structure becomes stronger and denser with LLM size.

fits_no_version.finding: Larger LLMs corrected their behaviour better overall. However, the resistance attributable to joint activation grew with size and was negative for most models below 4B.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Resistance from joint symptom-feature activation increases with LLM size, reversing sign around 4B parameters.

record.problems: The study provides no evidence on the claimed loss laws or compute-optimal allocation. For its own size-related measures, the text gives qualitative trends but not the numerical values or exact p-values; the full results are said to be in a public repository.

untested.parts: Held-out loss vs parameters, tokens or compute
Extrapolation of loss from small runs
Effect of depth/width on loss at fixed parameter count
Power laws in other modalities or training regimes
Downstream task performance vs scale or loss. Instruction-correction improving with size (Fig. 3E-left) is a related but unquantified observation, not a benchmark scaling fit
Dependence of exponents on setup and fitting choices

missing.what: Larger LLMs better follow corrective instructions overall (Fig. 3E-left). This is a size trend in instruction-following, not a loss or benchmark measure, so it bears on no version, but no row records it.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's T6/cites_only call is correct. Kaplan 2020 appears only as a citation for larger models being more capable. All size trends concern a different construct and are kept under fits_no_version.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss versus parameter count, tokens, or compute.
Prediction of larger-run held-out loss from power laws fitted on smaller runs.
Compute-optimal parameter and token allocation as a function of compute.
Effects of depth, width, and other architecture details on loss at fixed parameter count.
Power-law loss behavior in other modalities or training regimes.
Downstream performance as a function of scale or pretraining loss.
Dependence of loss-law exponents or compute-optimal splits on setup and fitting choices, and departures from a single power law.
